Born in Adams County, Pennsylvania. Served twice in the Civil War: in 1863 to 64 with Captain Robert Bell's Adams
County Cavalry (County B, 21st Pennsylvania Cavalry) , posted at Gettysburg after the battle,
and in 1865 with County G, 74th Pennsylvania Infantry, guarding the BandO Railroad in West Virginia.
Married Anna M. Ogden at Gettysburg on 12 May 1864.
In 1870 they were in Cumberland Township outside Gettysburg with four small children and Anna’s twelve-year-old half-brother
Robert Ogden; later in the decade they lived at Curwensville, Pennsylvania.
In 1878 they went west to Nashua, Illinois, near Franklin Grove, where Harry was born,
and in 1880 to a farm eight miles southeast of Ida Grove, Iowa, in Hayes Township.
They had twelve children, nine of whom outlived him.
A lifelong Methodist; after his death, the Ida Grove paper wrote, “many Ida Grove men have testified in reference
to his piety.” In old age he wintered at the Soldiers' Home in Hot Springs or in California.
The registers of the National Homes for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers show him admitted at Leavenworth,
Kansas, on 9 February 1909, a widower of seventy, five feet five and a half, dark-eyed,
with chronic rheumatism; he came back in for the winter that November, when a fellow veteran wrote to the Ida Grove
paper that his old captain had kept good quarters for him.
In 1910 he moved to the Battle Mountain Sanitarium at Hot Springs, South Dakota,
and checked himself in and out there most winters until 1918; by then he was deaf in both ears and had a weak heart.
He died suddenly at 84, on 4 July 1922, at his son W. G.'s ranch north of Rapid City,
and was taken home to Ida Grove to lie beside his wife.
Born at Gettysburg on 2 March, about 1842 (her obituary says 1843) , daughter of Francis C. Ogden and Eliza Polly.
In 1850 she was eight, at home in Cumberland Township outside Gettysburg; she lost her mother in 1856,
and at fifteen she was converted at Gettysburg.
In the summer of 1863 the battle was fought across the wheat her father had planted.
As her sister Rachel’s family told it to the Ida Grove paper in 1925, the two sisters walked up a hill near the house
to watch; Anna had put on boy’s clothes, thinking it safer.
Confederates came up and arrested her as a suspected spy, until an officer who had once stopped at the Ogden house
recognized both girls and let them go. Her younger brother Charles went to war with the 138th Pennsylvania in 1862
and was killed at Locust Grove, Virginia, in November 1863.
On 12 May 1864 she married Edward Clinton Wintrode, home from his first Civil War service.
In 1870 they had four little ones and her half-brother Robert, twelve, living with them.
They lived at Curwensville, Pennsylvania, then in 1878 went west to Nashua, Illinois,
and in 1880 to a farm in Hayes Township, eight miles southeast of Ida Grove, Iowa.
She bore twelve children, nine of whom survived her.
They came back east to visit family in the autumn of 1898.
In 1905 they moved into Ida Grove; she was ill from then on and bedridden for her last three weeks,
“always patient and cheerful,” the paper said.
She died at home in late November 1907, and the Methodist minister held the funeral at the house.
